ABSTRACT
Context. A knowledge of polarization properties of coherent radio waves escaping pulsar polar caps is crucial for calculating radiative
transfer through the magnetosphere and for obtaining specific predictions of observable radio properties.
Aims. We describe the pair cascades in the pulsar polar cap, and for the first time, determine the Stokes parameters of the escaping
radio waves from first-principle kinetic simulations for a pulsar with an inclination angle of the magnetic axis 60◦.
Methods. We utilize 3D particle-in-cell kinetic simulations that include quantum-electrodynamic pair cascades in a charge-limited
flow from the stellar surface.
Results. Our model provides a quantitative and qualitative explanation of the observed pulsar radio powers and spectra, the pulse
profiles and polarization curves, their temporal variability, the strong Stokes L and weak Stokes V polarization components, as well
as the fact that linear polarization decreases with frequency and the non-existence of a radius to frequency relationship. We find that
the radio emission from the polar cap can produce a diverse range of observed pulsar properties, including single or double peaked
profiles. Most of the Stokes V curves from our simulations appear to be antisymmetric, but symmetric curves are also present at some
viewing angles. Although the PA swing of the radiation from the polar cap can be fitted by the rotating vector model (RVM) for
most viewing angles, the angles obtained from the RVM do not correspond to the angular distance of the observer from the magnetic
axis. Instead, the PA is directly related to the plasma flows in the polar cap and not to the dipole geometry of the magnetic field. The
observed range of other polarization features, in addition to our results, can be explained by propagation effects which are not part of
the simulation. Furthermore, we find that the radiation is associated with the escaping plasma bunches and that it can propagate freely
along flux channels of low plasma density, in addition to being reflected on the channel boundaries of high plasma density.
Conclusions. Our simulations demonstrate that pair discharges close to the surface of the pulsar polar cap are responsible for the
radio emission of pulsars and determine the majority of its typically observed properties. The usage of RVM for estimations of the
magnetic field geometry from observations needs to be reevaluated.
Key words. Stars: neutron – pulsars: general – Plasmas – Instabilities – Relativistic processes – Methods: numerical
1. Introduction
Most of the coherent radio emission of rotation-powered pulsars is driven by pair cascades and originates in or close to polar
caps (Ruderman & Sutherland 1975; Cheng & Ruderman 1977).
The initial characteristics of the coherent radio waves that escape the polar cap have been the subject of research over many
years (Melrose & Rafat 2017; Melrose et al. 2020; Philippov &
Kramer 2022), but this has not yielded a final and satisfactory
model so far. The initial properties of the emission are however
essential for the calculation of the radiative transfer in pulsar
radio emission models (Petrova & Lyubarskii 2000; Beskin &
Philippov 2012; Hakobyan et al. 2017; Cao et al. 2024a) and
any interpretation of the observed polarization (Stinebring et al.
1984; Bilous et al. 2016; Oswald et al. 2023; Cao et al. 2024b).
The pair discharge cascades in polar caps play an essential
role in many plasma processes of pulsars. They cause the emission of a wide spectral range of electromagnetic waves (Hobbs
et al. 2004; Daugherty & Harding 1996; Pétri 2019; Giraud &
Pétri 2021), instabilities resulting in coherent radio emissions
(Asseo & Melikidze 1998; Melikidze et al. 2000; Gil et al. 2004),
particle acceleration (Daugherty & Harding 1982), relativistic
plasma outflows (Pétri 2022), filling of the neutron star magnetosphere with pair plasma (Tomczak & Pétri 2023), and neutron
star heating (Zhang & Harding 2000; Gonzalez & Reisenegger
2010; Köpp et al. 2023).
Various coherent radio emission mechanisms in or near pulsar polar caps have been proposed since the discovery of the first
pulsar; for a summary, see Melrose & Gedalin (1999); Eilek &
Hankins (2016); Melrose et al. (2020) and references therein.
The mechanisms included the coherent curvature radiation produced by charge solitons produced by relativistic streaming instabilities (Melikidze & Pataraya 1980; Melikidze et al. 2000;
Mitra 2017; Manthei et al. 2021; Benáˇcek et al. 2021b,a, 2024a;
Mitra et al. 2024), relativistic plasma emission by wave–wave
interaction (Weatherall 1997), linear acceleration emission by
particles undergoing acceleration along the magnetic field direction (Melrose et al. 2009; Melrose & Luo 2009; Benáˇcek
et al. 2023) or in an arbitrary direction to the magnetic field in
free-electron maser emission (Fung & Kuijpers 2004), anomalous Doppler emission (Lyutikov et al. 1999), and electron cyclotron/synchrotron maser emission (Kazbegi et al. 1991; Labaj
et al. 2024). Nonetheless, there is no decisive observational evidence favouring one of these mechanisms so far.

Philippov et al. (2020). They suggested a novel radio emission
mechanism where charge inhomogeneities in the intermittently
created pair plasma produce an electric field component, which
can be classified as O-mode polarized electromagnetic waves,
which then propagate together with the plasma along the magnetic field lines. The wave generation was confirmed by their
particle-in-cell (PIC) kinetic simulations (Philippov et al. 2020),
which showed broadband spectra of the radiation in a frequency
range commensurate with the observed pulsar spectra.

were studied by Cruz et al. (2021a) by considering pair cascades
along diverging magnetic field lines. They detected two peaks in
the outflowing Poynting flux of electromagnetic plasma waves,
which were interpreted as being potentially associated with the
core and conal components of pulsar radio emissions (Rankin
1990, 1993). The excitation of electromagnetic waves in pair
discharges was also confirmed by global 2D PIC simulations of

who have demonstrated that electromagnetic waves can also be
generated in other magnetospheric regions. The damping of such
waves during the discharges was studied by Tolman et al. (2022).

damping of the waves becomes linear in time. Therefore, these
O-mode waves could still carry enough energy when they decouple from the plasma when the plasma density drops at a certain
distance. The waves become vacuum electromagnetic waves that

which then propagate together with the plasma along the magnetic field lines. The wave generation was confirmed by their
particle-in-cell (PIC) kinetic simulations (Philippov et al. 2020),
which showed broadband spectra of the radiation in a frequency
range commensurate with the observed pulsar spectra.
The kinetic effects in the polar cap plasma of aligned pulsars
were studied by Cruz et al. (2021a) by considering pair cascades
along diverging magnetic field lines. They detected two peaks in
the outflowing Poynting flux of electromagnetic plasma waves,
which were interpreted as being potentially associated with the
core and conal components of pulsar radio emissions (Rankin
1990, 1993). The excitation of electromagnetic waves in pair
discharges was also confirmed by global 2D PIC simulations of
the aligned rotator’s magnetosphere by Bransgrove et al. (2023),
who have demonstrated that electromagnetic waves can also be
generated in other magnetospheric regions. The damping of such
waves during the discharges was studied by Tolman et al. (2022).
They showed that after initially strong exponential damping, the
damping of the waves becomes linear in time. Therefore, these
O-mode waves could still carry enough energy when they decouple from the plasma when the plasma density drops at a certain
distance. The waves become vacuum electromagnetic waves that
could be observed as pulsar radio emission.
Including pair cascades in PIC simulations clearly results in
a more physically accurate description of the magnetospheric
properties. Benáˇcek et al. (2024b) found by using 2D simulations that radio waves can be transported away from the polar
cap in Poynting flux transport channels when typical profiles of
magnetospheric currents across the polar cap are considered for
various magnetic axis inclinations. The channels consist of magnetic field lines where the plasma density is low as the result
of locally small parallel electric fields and currents that do not
support the generation of pair cascades. The plasma frequency
on these field lines is well below the frequencies of the generated electromagnetic waves, and these waves can then propagate along the field lines without significant absorption. Benáˇcek
et al. (2024b) also showed that the Poynting flux associated with
dense plasma bunches decrease with the distance from the star
while the flux in the Poynting flux channel shows no significant
decrease. Moreover, the obtained spectrum of waves in the channel resembles the typical radio pulsar spectrum. More detailed
modeling of the radiative transfer is however required before
one can decide how the radiation escapes the magnetosphere.
Chernoglazov et al. (2024) studied the cascades in 3D, finding
the 3D polar cap structure and coherence scales of the cascades
to be of the order of the electric gap height.
The detailed properties of the electromagnetic radiation escaping the polar cap in the form of the Poynting flux are essential
for specific model predictions about observable radio frequency
characteristics, but they remain unclear in 2D simulations. The
polarization vector lies in the plane of the simulation domain
by definition for 2D simulations; hence, one cannot obtain any
information about the polarization properties from such simulations. To the best of our knowledge, no polarization studies for
pulsars have employed 3D kinetic simulations before.
In this paper, we focus on the polarization properties of the
electromagnetic radiation which escapes the pulsar polar cap.
The polarization properties are obtained from scaled 3D PIC
fully-kinetic simulations that describe the pair discharges and the
associated wave–particle interactions. The pair creation is driven
by the magnetospheric currents. Their profile across the polar
cap is obtained from known global general-relativistic force-free
simulations of the magnetosphere.
This paper is structured as follows. In Section 2, we discuss
the plasma and numerical setup of the pair cascades in the pulsar
polar cap. Section 3 describes the plasma properties and shows
the polarization properties of the escaping waves when the quasiperiodic nature of the cascades has established itself. We discuss
the obtained properties in Section 4 and describe the main polarization properties in Section 5.
2. Methods
In this paper, we study the polar cap region of pulsars, which

is triggered when the plasma density drops below the threshold
density for pair annihilation, which depends on the particle energy
and the density.
